templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
No punctuation between subject and verb
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a noun-phrase opener
items.passage: In 1938, a man excavating a cistern in the town of Igbo-Ukwu in southeastern Nigeria encountered a cache of buried ______ ornamented vessels, ceremonial altar stands, and pendants cast around the ninth century CE, the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are among the oldest surviving metal castings from West Africa.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1938 ... encountered a cache of buried objects” is a complete sentence. The noun phrase “Intricately ornamented vessels, ceremonial altar stands, and pendants cast around the ninth century CE” describes the subject of the next sentence, “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes,” which has its own verb, “are.” A period is needed between the two independent clauses.

A.recipe: comma splice (opener read as an appositive to clause 1)
A.why_wrong: The comma makes the list look like a description of “objects,” but “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: “That were” attaches the noun phrase to the first clause, which still leaves “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are ...” joined to it with only a comma.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “objects intricately ornamented vessels” runs the two clauses together, and the comma before “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes” then splices them.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (West African bronze casting). Band 7: a 14-word noun-phrase opener with an internal series that reads as an appositive to clause 1's last noun until “the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are” arrives 15 words after the blank (0fa289a7 / 940ff6f7 shape).

band7.why: 0fa289a7 / 940ff6f7 shape with the a872c60a menu (period key, splice, glued, added 'that were'): a 14-word noun-phrase opener with an internal series reads as an appositive to 'objects' until 'the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are' arrives 15 words after the blank; one 46-word run.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a Because-clause opener
items.passage: Unlike conventional white paint, which reflects only 80 to 90 percent of incoming sunlight, the paint that engineer Xiulin Ruan and his colleagues unveiled in 2021 stays cool even under a midday ______ the paint reflects roughly 98 percent of sunlight while radiating heat as infrared light, a coated surface can remain cooler than the surrounding air.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Unlike conventional white paint ... under a midday sun” is a complete sentence. The next sentence opens with the dependent clause “Because the paint reflects ... infrared light,” and its main clause is “a coated surface can remain cooler than the surrounding air.” A period is needed between the two sentences.

A.recipe: comma splice (subordinate clause read as part of clause 1)
A.why_wrong: The “because” clause seems to explain the first clause, but “a coated surface can remain cooler” is a second independent clause, so the sentence joins two independent clauses with only a comma.

B.recipe: comma splice (subordinate clause glued to clause 1)
B.why_wrong: Without punctuation the “because” clause attaches to the first clause, and the comma after “light” then joins “a coated surface can remain cooler ...” to it, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “That” starts a relative clause that never gets a verb of its own, so the sentence breaks down; it also leaves the two main clauses joined with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: science and technology (radiative cooling paint). Band 7: clause 2 opens with a subordinator (615f001e move), so the comma and no-mark versions read naturally until the main clause's subject appears about 15 words later. No semicolon or colon option: both would be acceptable before a because-clause opener.

band7.why: 615f001e move: clause 2 opens with 'Because', so the comma and no-mark versions read as a natural because-clause on clause 1 until 'a coated surface' arrives 15 words after the blank. 56-word run, but every part does work (the 80 to 90 percent baseline gives '98 percent' its point; the infrared radiation is what makes 'cooler than the surrounding air' true), so not trimmed.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a gerund subject
items.passage: Hoping to curb dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, researchers released mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia, a bacterium that prevents the virus from replicating, across half of 24 designated neighborhoods in Yogyakarta, ______ Wolbachia into the local mosquito population reduced dengue incidence there by roughly 77 percent, the team reported in 2021.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Hoping to curb dengue ... in Yogyakarta, Indonesia” is a complete sentence. The next sentence has the gerund phrase “Introducing Wolbachia into the local mosquito population” as its subject and “reduced” as its verb. A period is needed to separate the two independent clauses.

B.recipe: comma splice (gerund subject read as a participial phrase)
B.why_wrong: The comma makes “introducing ...” look like a modifier of the first clause, but it is the subject of “reduced,” so two independent clauses are joined with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the first clause runs straight into the second clause's subject, “Introducing Wolbachia ...,” which has the verb “reduced.”

D.why_wrong: “By” turns the subject into a phrase about how the mosquitoes were released, so the verb “reduced” is left with no subject.

items.notes: Subject: science (public health, mosquito-borne disease). Band 6: gerund subject of clause 2 (73a6603c shape); the verb that resolves it comes 7 words after the blank, and the city-country comma (Yogyakarta, Indonesia,) makes the comma option look natural.

band7.why: 73a6603c shape: gerund subject resolved by 'reduced' 7 words after the blank; the city-country comma makes B look natural. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, colon before an explanation
items.passage: Visitors to an art gallery typically expect simply to contemplate whatever is on display. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s 1992 exhibition Untitled (Free) asked its visitors to do more than ______ he converted the New York gallery’s back office into a makeshift kitchen and invited them to linger, eat the curry he prepared, and converse with strangers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The adverb “however” belongs to the first clause: the exhibition asking visitors to do more than look contrasts with the previous sentence, in which visitors expect only to contemplate what is displayed. The comma sets “however” off from that clause, and the colon introduces the second clause, which explains what more the exhibition asked of them.

A.why_wrong: A comma after “however” cannot join the two independent clauses “Thai artist ... however” and “he converted ... with strangers.”

B.why_wrong: Nothing marks the boundary after “however,” so the two independent clauses run together.

D.why_wrong: Placing “however” at the start of the second clause signals that converting the office into a kitchen and inviting visitors to eat and talk contrasts with asking them to do more than look, but it is exactly the “more” that the first clause describes.

items.notes: Subject: arts (relational art, 1992 gallery show). Band 7: adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence; colon variant (84658166); the strongest distractor is the textbook `; however,` placement, wrong only by meaning. No `however;` option, since a semicolon after however would also be acceptable.

band7.why: 84658166 / c15069eb menu: ', however:' closes clause 1 and answers sentence 1 (visitors expect only to contemplate); D's textbook '; however,' is wrong only by meaning, since the kitchen is the 'more' that clause 1 announces, not a contrast with it. No ', however;' option, which would also be acceptable.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, period before the next sentence
items.passage: Many poems by the Vietnamese poet Hồ Xuân Hương appear at first to describe unremarkable things, such as a ripening jackfruit or a swing at a spring festival. The poems are rarely as innocent as they seem, ______ frequently conceal a second, mischievous meaning that ridicules the pompous scholars and monks of her era.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The poems are rarely as innocent as they seem, however” is a complete sentence, and “however” signals the contrast with the previous sentence. “They frequently conceal a second, mischievous meaning ...” is another independent clause, so a period is needed after “however.”

A.why_wrong: “However” is not a conjunction, so a comma after it joins two independent clauses with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation after “however.”

D.recipe: conjunction without comma, adverb glued to the conjunction
D.why_wrong: “But” needs a comma before it to join these long clauses, and it signals a second contrast that the text does not contain.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Vietnamese poetry, double meanings). Band 6: the period-after-adverb shape of 2bb7416a (not used in b1 or b2); the decision rests on reading “however” as part of clause 1.

band7.why: 2bb7416a menu ('however. They' key, splice, fused, 'however but'): the decision is reading 'however' as part of clause 1, with no logic-wrong option. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Colon before a specified item, then a period in the same option
items.passage: Between about 1075 and 1220 CE, the kingdom of Mapungubwe in southern Africa prospered by trading gold and ivory with merchants from the Indian Ocean coast. A grave on the kingdom’s royal hill contained what is now its most celebrated ______ from gold foil tacked over a wooden core, it has become an emblem of the region’s precolonial history.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The colon follows a complete clause (“A grave ... contained what is now its most celebrated artifact”) and introduces the item it names, the golden rhinoceros. The period then ends that sentence, and the next one opens with the participial phrase “Crafted from gold foil tacked over a wooden core,” which describes its subject, “it.”

A.why_wrong: Commas alone leave “it has become an emblem ...” joined to the first independent clause with only a comma.

B.why_wrong: The new sentence would begin “The golden rhinoceros, crafted from ...,” and then add a second subject, “it,” before the verb “has become.”

C.recipe: semicolon before a clause with two subjects
C.why_wrong: What follows the semicolon has the same doubled subject (“the golden rhinoceros ... it has become”), so it is not a standard independent clause.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Mapungubwe, southern Africa). Band 7: two slots in one option (colon then period), 3a2d77d7 shape; three distractors are partly right at one slot. Review: second sentence now opens with a past participle (“Crafted from ...”) rather than 3a2d77d7’s “A relatively quiet instrument,” so the skeleton is not a copy.

fixes: options and sentence 2: opener changed from 'A small figure crafted from' to the participle 'Crafted from', so the second sentence no longer copies 3a2d77d7's skeleton; explanation and B why_wrong updated

band7.why: 3a2d77d7 move: colon then period in one option, three distractors each right at one slot, and the doubled subject that kills B and C ('the golden rhinoceros ... it') shows only 9 words after the blank.

items.subtype: No comma before a restrictive that-clause
items.passage: Whereas many Western writing guides treat conflict as the engine of every plot, kishōtenketsu is a four-part model for ______ writers in China, Japan, and Korea have long employed: an introduction, a development, an apparently unrelated twist, and a conclusion that reconciles the preceding parts.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That many writers in China, Japan, and Korea have long employed” is a restrictive clause: it identifies which model for storytelling the text means. No punctuation goes between “storytelling” and “that,” and the colon after “employed” then introduces the four parts.

A.why_wrong: A comma is not used before “that” when it introduces a clause essential to the noun it modifies.

B.why_wrong: “Many writers ... have long employed” is not a complete sentence, because the verb “employed” still needs its object. A colon can’t follow it, and a colon can’t separate a verb from its object, so the list after the colon can’t complete it.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “many writers ... have long employed” lacks the object of “employed,” and the colon after it can’t supply one, since a colon can’t separate a verb from its object.

items.notes: Subject: literature (narrative structure). Band 6: restrictive that-clause with the omitted-object trap of 5ef9fc48.

fixes: B and D why_wrong: name the rule (a colon can't follow an incomplete clause or separate a verb from its object), since the list after the colon looks like an object

band7.why: 5ef9fc48 menu and move: restrictive that-clause whose verb lacks an object, so the period and semicolon options leave no clause; local. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (word as word) followed by a nonrestrictive which-clause
items.passage: In 2007, Colombian artist Doris Salcedo created a jagged crack running the full length of the concrete floor in the entrance hall of London’s Tate Modern museum. She took the installation’s title from the Hebrew ______ was once used to identify enemies by their inability to pronounce it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Shibboleth” identifies which Hebrew word is meant, so it is a restrictive appositive and takes no comma after “word.” The clause “which was once used ...” adds information about that one word, so it is set off with a comma, placed inside the closing quotation mark.

B.recipe: comma intrudes into a restrictive appositive; missing comma before a nonrestrictive clause
B.why_wrong: The comma separates “word” from the word it names, and no comma sets off the which-clause.

C.recipe: missing comma before a nonrestrictive clause
C.why_wrong: The which-clause adds information about a single, already identified word, so it needs a comma.

D.why_wrong: The commas treat “shibboleth” as removable, but without it the sentence would not say which Hebrew word supplied the title.

items.notes: Subject: arts (installation art). Band 7: non-person restrictive appositive (59a246dc) plus a second slot after it (comma before which); D’s polite commas around the word are the band-7 trap. Review: sentence 1 rewritten, its appositive had landed after “museum.”

fixes: sentence 1: the appositive 'a jagged crack ...' sat after 'museum' and read as describing it; rewritten as two sentences (the crack, then the title), which also splits a 45-word sentence; dropped the filler 'vast'

band7.why: 59a246dc shape (non-person restrictive appositive 'the Hebrew word shibboleth') plus a second slot ruled by a different rule, the comma before the nonrestrictive which-clause; D's polite commas around the word are CB's band-7 trap (S4_restrictive is local at every band).

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair around an element that contains its own comma supplement
items.passage: In 1998, divers searching for sea cucumbers off Indonesia’s Belitung Island found the wreck of a ninth-century Arab trading ship. Its cargo—some 60,000 bowls, ewers, and other ceramic pieces from ______ is the largest assemblage of Tang dynasty goods ever recovered from a single site.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: China, most of them made in Changsha,
China, most of them made in Changsha—
China—most of them made in Changsha,
China, most of them made in Changsha
items.explanation: The dash after “cargo” opens a supplementary element describing the cargo, so a dash must close it before the verb “is.” Inside that element, the comma after “China” sets off the smaller supplement “most of them made in Changsha.”

A.why_wrong: The commas inside the element (“bowls, ewers, and other”) make a closing comma look natural, but an element opened with a dash after “cargo” must be closed with a dash.

C.why_wrong: The dash after “China” closes the dash element too early, leaving “most of them made in Changsha,” stranded between the dash and the verb “is.”

D.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the element opened after “cargo” never ends, and it runs straight into the verb “is.”

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Indian Ocean trade). Band 7: two levels inside the dash element (6e071432 move, without its wording); opening dash 9 words before the blank, with a comma list inside the element that makes the comma close (A) look natural. Review: cut the idle “likely bound for the Persian Gulf,” split the 56-word sentence and moved the opening dash from 4 to 9 words before the blank.

fixes: cut the idle 'likely bound for the Persian Gulf' and split the 56-word sentence; opening dash moved from 4 to 9 words before the blank, with a comma list inside the element (band-7 S3_dash_pair recipe); options, explanation and why_wrong rewritten

band7.why: After the fix: 6e071432 move, a comma-set supplement inside a dash element whose opening dash sits 9 words before the blank, with a comma list inside it that makes the comma close (A) look natural; options mix the two levels. As drafted the partner was 4 words away, which read band 6.

items.subtype: Complex series: semicolon after an item with a supplement, comma inside the option
items.passage: Barcelona created its first superblock, a grid of nine city blocks, in 2016. Within it, municipal planners converted intersections into ______ reduced the speed limit to 10 kilometers per hour; and closed the interior streets to through traffic, admitting only residents, deliveries, and emergency vehicles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: plazas, many with benches and playgrounds;
plazas many with benches and playgrounds;
plazas; many with benches and playgrounds,
plazas, many with benches and playgrounds,
items.explanation: The planners did three things, and the items contain commas, so semicolons separate them, as the semicolon before “and closed” shows. Within the first item, a comma sets off the supplement “many with benches and playgrounds” from “plazas,” and a semicolon ends the item.

B.why_wrong: The phrase “many with benches and playgrounds” describes the plazas and must be set off from “plazas” with a comma.

C.why_wrong: The semicolon cuts the first item in half, and the comma after “playgrounds” fails to separate it from the second item.

D.recipe: commas only in a complex series
D.why_wrong: A comma after “playgrounds” does not match the semicolon used later between the second and third items.

items.notes: Subject: social science (urban planning). Band 7: blank in item 1, the revealing semicolon comes 9 words later, and the option carries a second rule (comma before an absolute supplement), db24ecc9 / 9c3630b9 shape.

band7.why: db24ecc9 / 9c3630b9 shape: blank closes item 1 of a semicolon series, the revealing semicolon comes 9 words later, and the option carries a second rule (comma before 'many with benches and playgrounds'); D, the comma version, is CB's band-7 S5 trap.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: Damascus steel, used for centuries to forge swords in the Middle East, is renowned for its strength and its distinctive wavy patterns. A seventeenth-century saber that materials scientist Marianne Reibold’s team examined under an electron ______ contained carbon nanotubes, structures typically associated with modern nanotechnology.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the long noun phrase “A seventeenth-century saber that ... examined under an electron microscope,” and its verb is “contained.” No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.

A.recipe: comma intrudes between subject and verb
A.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the subject “A seventeenth-century saber ... microscope” from its verb “contained.”

B.why_wrong: The words before the semicolon are a subject with no main verb, so they are not an independent clause.

D.why_wrong: A single dash has no partner here and splits the subject from its verb.

items.notes: Subject: science and history (materials science, historic steel). Plan asked band 7, but S4_subj_verb has no band-7 official items, so written as a strong band 6 (15-word subject with a restrictive clause before the blank, comma tempting) and band_target set to 6.

band7.why: S4_subj_verb has no band-7 officials: strong band 6 in the f868d438 (3.13) shape, a 15-word subject carrying a restrictive clause before the blank. band_target already 6.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and but
items.passage: Brazilian writer Clarice Lispector’s novel The Hour of the Star (1977) is narrated by a struggling author who sets out to recount the story of Macabéa, an impoverished young typist living in Rio de ______ he repeatedly interrupts that narrative with digressions about himself and about the difficulty of portraying her.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Brazilian writer ... living in Rio de Janeiro” and “he repeatedly interrupts ... portraying her” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and shows the contrast.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation or conjunction.

C.why_wrong: When “but” joins two long independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Brazilian novel).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short prepositional opener
items.passage: Male tree-hole frogs in Borneo serenade females from cavities in tree trunks that are partially filled with ______ a 2002 study, biologists Björn Lardner and Maklarin bin Lakim found that each male adjusts his call to match his cavity’s resonant frequency, which fluctuates as rainwater accumulates or evaporates.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Male tree-hole frogs ... partially filled with water” is a complete sentence. “In a 2002 study” is an introductory phrase that begins the next sentence, whose subject and verb are “biologists ... found.” A period is needed between the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma joins two independent clauses, the second beginning with the introductory phrase “in a 2002 study.”

C.why_wrong: “In a 2002 study” attaches to the first clause, which leaves “biologists ... found” joined to it with only a comma.

D.why_wrong: “And” joining two long independent clauses needs a comma before it.

items.notes: Subject: science (animal behavior, acoustics).

items.subtype: Comma inside a closing quotation mark before a sentence appositive
items.passage: In 2017, classicist Emily Wilson became the first woman to publish an English translation of Homer’s Odyssey, the ancient Greek epic about a warrior’s long voyage home. Her version contains exactly as many lines as the original ______ constraint that compelled her to make her English as economical as Homer’s verse.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause ends with “the original poem.” What follows, “a constraint that ...,” is a noun phrase that comments on the whole clause, not a clause itself. A comma separates the main clause from this supplementary phrase.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “a constraint that ...” is a noun phrase.

C.why_wrong: Joining the noun phrase with “and” results in an illogical sentence that says her version contains a constraint as well as lines; the matching line count is itself the constraint.

D.why_wrong: “A constraint that ... Homer’s verse” has no main verb, so it cannot stand as a sentence.

items.notes: Subject: literature (translation). Trailing sentence appositive (2.24 shape, without its quotation), not the -ing tail used in b1 and b2.

fixes: C why_wrong: now matches CB's rationale for the 'and' recipe (3ed5ebb4): the sentence says her version contains a constraint, which is illogical

items.subtype: Opening a comma pair around an appositive title
items.passage: Senegalese writer Ousmane Sembène turned from fiction to filmmaking in the 1960s, hoping to reach African audiences unable to read his French-language novels. His first feature ______ Black Girl (1966), follows a young woman from Dakar who becomes increasingly isolated while employed as a domestic servant by a French family.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The title “Black Girl (1966)” is a nonessential appositive naming his first feature film, and the comma after “(1966)” closes it. A matching comma is needed after “film” to open the pair.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma after “film,” the comma after “(1966)” falls between the subject and its verb, “follows.”

B.why_wrong: A dash cannot open an element that is closed with a comma.

D.why_wrong: “His first feature film” is not a complete clause, so a colon cannot follow it, and the comma after “(1966)” would then split the subject from “follows.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (African cinema). Partner comma 3 words after the blank.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory appositive
items.passage: Hummingbirds were long assumed to draw nectar up their tongues through capillary action, the way water climbs a narrow tube. A Colombian biologist who has filmed hummingbirds at high speed as they ______ Alejandro Rico-Guevara discovered instead that the tongue functions like a pump, its grooves springing open in the nectar and drawing it inside.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A Colombian biologist who has filmed hummingbirds at high speed as they feed” is an introductory phrase that describes the subject, “Alejandro Rico-Guevara.” A comma separates it from the main clause, “Alejandro Rico-Guevara discovered instead ....”

A.why_wrong: The introductory phrase has no main verb, so it cannot stand before a semicolon.

B.why_wrong: A comma is needed to separate the long introductory phrase from the subject it describes.

C.why_wrong: “A Colombian biologist ... as they feed” is not a complete sentence.

items.notes: Subject: science (animal feeding mechanics). Introductory appositive (2.25 shape), unlike b2's participial opener.

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses
items.passage: In 2007, archaeologist Julio Mercader’s team reported discovering 4,300-year-old stone hammers in the rainforest of Côte d’Ivoire. Chimpanzees, not humans, had most likely wielded them to crack ______ the stones were considerably heavier than the hammers that people in the region use, and starch residues on them came from nuts that local chimpanzees still consume.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Chimpanzees ... wielded them to crack nuts” and “the stones were considerably heavier ... still consume” are both independent clauses. A semicolon is used to join two independent clauses without a conjunction.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation.

D.why_wrong: “And” joining two long independent clauses needs a comma before it.

items.notes: Subject: science and history (primate archaeology).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: In 2007, Uruguay launched Plan Ceibal, an initiative that provides a free laptop ______ every student in the country’s public elementary schools. By 2009, the program had reached all of these students, making Uruguay the first country to supply a computer to every public elementary school student.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “To” is a preposition, and “every student” is its object. No punctuation should come between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon cannot separate a preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate a preposition from its object.

D.why_wrong: A single dash has no role between a preposition and its object.

items.notes: Subject: social science (education policy).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a noun and its prepositional modifier
items.passage: For centuries, the Akan peoples of present-day Ghana used gold dust as currency, measuring quantities against small brass weights. Artisans cast many of these weights in the ______ of animals, people, and everyday objects, and some were designed to illustrate traditional proverbs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Of animals, people, and everyday objects” tells what shapes the weights were cast in, so it belongs to the noun “shapes.” No punctuation should separate a noun from the phrase that completes it.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; “Artisans cast many of these weights in the shapes” is not one.

B.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate “shapes” from the phrase “of animals ...” that completes it.

D.why_wrong: A single dash has no role between a noun and its modifier.

items.notes: Subject: arts and history (West African metalwork).

items.subtype: Direct question at the start of the text
items.passage: How ______ Biologist Giacomo Bernardi documented one answer off the coast of Palau in 2009: an orange-dotted tuskfish excavated a clam from the sand, transported it to a rock, and repeatedly smashed it against the rock until the shell fractured.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: a fish can break open a clam?
can a fish break open a clam.
a fish can break open a clam.
can a fish break open a clam?
items.explanation: The sentence that begins with “How” is a direct question, so the helping verb comes before the subject (“can a fish”) and the sentence ends with a question mark.

A.recipe: statement order with a question mark
A.why_wrong: A direct question needs inverted order: “can a fish,” not “a fish can.”

B.recipe: question order ending in a period
B.why_wrong: A direct question ends with a question mark, not a period.

C.why_wrong: “How a fish can break open a clam.” is neither a question nor a complete sentence.

items.notes: Subject: science (tool use in fish). Sentence-initial question (1.30 shape); b2 used a question after a colon.

items.subtype: Relative clause in statement order, ending with a period
items.passage: Tsitsi Dangarembga’s 1988 novel Nervous Conditions follows a Zimbabwean girl who leaves her family’s homestead to attend a mission school. The book’s title comes from a phrase ______ In it, Sartre describes the situation of colonized people as “a nervous condition.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Jean-Paul Sartre used in a 1961 preface.
did Jean-Paul Sartre use in a 1961 preface?
Jean-Paul Sartre used in a 1961 preface?
did Jean-Paul Sartre use in a 1961 preface.
items.explanation: “Jean-Paul Sartre used in a 1961 preface” is a relative clause describing “a phrase”; the sentence is a statement, not a question. It uses statement word order (“Sartre used”) and ends with a period.

B.recipe: question order with a question mark
B.why_wrong: The sentence makes a statement about the title, so it needs neither inverted order nor a question mark.

C.why_wrong: The sentence is a statement, so it ends with a period.

D.recipe: question order in a relative clause
D.why_wrong: A relative clause uses statement order: “Sartre used,” not “did Sartre use.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Zimbabwean novel). Relative clause frame (1.24), unlike b1's embedded why-question.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: In the 1960s, Brazilian artist Hélio Oiticica began creating Parangolés, capes constructed from layers of fabric and plastic. Although the capes could be displayed on a gallery ______ Oiticica intended them to be worn by samba dancers, whose movements would animate the colorful layers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Although the capes could be displayed on a gallery wall” is a dependent clause that introduces the main clause, “Oiticica intended them to be worn by samba dancers.” A comma separates the introductory clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: The “although” clause is dependent, so it cannot stand before a semicolon.

C.why_wrong: A comma is needed after this introductory clause.

D.why_wrong: “Although the capes could be displayed on a gallery wall.” is not a complete sentence.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Brazilian art).

items.subtype: Commas between items in a simple series
items.passage: On the last Saturday of each month, many adults in Rwanda participate in umuganda, a morning of mandatory community service. Depending on their neighborhood’s needs, participants might help build a ______ clear drainage ditches, or repair a road before gathering to discuss local concerns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three activities: building a classroom, clearing drainage ditches, and repairing a road. Commas separate the items in a simple series like this one.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, “a classroom” and “clear drainage ditches” run together.

B.why_wrong: Semicolons separate series items only when the items contain commas, and the other items here are separated by commas.

D.why_wrong: A colon cannot separate one item in a series from the next.

items.notes: Subject: social science (civic practice).

items.subtype: No comma before a restrictive that-clause
items.passage: In 1650, Spanish painter Diego Velázquez completed a portrait of Juan de Pareja, the enslaved man who served as his studio assistant. Pareja was eventually freed and became an accomplished painter in his own right. His best-known work is The Calling of Saint Matthew, a ______ includes a self-portrait.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That includes a self-portrait” is a restrictive clause that tells which kind of painting the work is. No comma comes before “that,” and “that” is needed as the subject of “includes.”

A.recipe: missing word, comma before the verb
A.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verb “includes” has no subject, and the comma separates “a painting” from it.

B.why_wrong: Without “that,” the sentence reads “a painting includes ...,” which has two verbs and no way to connect them.

C.why_wrong: A comma is not used before “that” when it introduces an essential clause.

items.notes: Subject: arts and history (Spanish painting).
